content.text: Pulling the SCOPe 2.08 hierarchy together now. I've confirmed all three families sit in the same superfamily, so I'm writing the answer.

answers.answer: Read them as three separate families inside one superfamily, so the link is remote homology. In SCOPe 2.08 (checked live) all three belong to superfamily c.2.1, 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (sunid 51735), in fold c.2, 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (sunid 51734), class c. The three families are: 'Alcohol dehydrogenase-like, C-terminal domain' (c.2.1.2, sunid 51736), 'CoA-binding domain' (c.2.1.9, sunid 51900) and 'Potassium channel NAD-binding domain' (c.2.1.11, sunid 63944). Note that the parent of sunid 63944 is 51735 and its sccs is c.2.1.9 in the search index. The children listing for 51735 gives different family numbering, so treat the sunids as the stable identifiers and re-check the sccs strings in the release you use. Same superfamily means SCOP judges a probable common evolutionary origin from structure and shared features: a common Rossmann-like βαβ nucleotide-binding core and a conserved dinucleotide-binding mode. That is a deeper and weaker relationship than same family. SCOPe families group clearer relationships, such as sequence-detectable homology or close functional and structural similarity. The separate families therefore signal clear divergence in sequence, function and often substrate and cofactor chemistry. A biologist should not read the shared superfamily as shared function, shared cofactor specificity or a shared catalytic mechanism. The ADH-like domain is the NAD(P)-binding half of zinc-dependent alcohol dehydrogenases and related medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases, an oxidoreductase catalytic role. The CoA-binding domain is found in succinyl-CoA synthetase-type proteins and related proteins. Its Rossmann-like fold is used for CoA or nucleotide binding, not as a classic NAD(P) redox domain. The potassium channel NAD-binding domain, an RCK-type regulatory domain such as the Rck domain of Kch, is a ligand-sensing regulatory module of an ion channel. It is not an oxidoreductase catalytic domain. So the same fold can give redox catalysis, CoA-related enzymology, or ligand-gated regulation. Practical limits: do not transfer EC numbers, substrate, cofactor preference, catalytic residues or active-site annotation across these families on SCOPe placement alone. Do not use a member of one family as a modelling template for another's function or ligand-binding details. Backbone-level modelling of the core may be reasonable, but loops, the domain's role in the whole protein, oligomerisation and ligand-binding residues will differ. Superfamily membership alone is not evidence of orthology, and fold-level c.2 similarity would be weaker still. Check family-specific evidence before drawing conclusions: sequence alignment and conserved motifs (for example the Gly-rich dinucleotide-binding loop and acidic residue binding the ribose), HMM or profile hits, structure comparison, domain architecture, ligand-bound structures, and functional assays or literature. Also check whether the SCOPe domain is a single domain of a multidomain protein (ADH has a separate catalytic domain; the channel domain sits in a larger channel complex), since the function belongs to the whole protein context. When choosing representatives, pick one per family and not one per superfamily, since the families differ in function.

answers.answer: Read them as three separate families inside one superfamily, so the link is remote homology. In SCOPe 2.08 (checked live) all three belong to superfamily c.2.1, 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (sunid 51735), in fold c.2, 'NAD(P)-binding Rossmann-fold domains' (sunid 51734), class c. The three families are: 'Alcohol dehydrogenase-like, C-terminal domain' (c.2.1.2, sunid 51736), 'CoA-binding domain' (c.2.1.9, sunid 51900) and 'Potassium channel NAD-binding domain' (c.2.1.11, sunid 63944). Note that the parent of sunid 63944 is 51735 and its sccs is c.2.1.9 in the search index. The children listing for 51735 gives different family numbering, so treat the sunids as the stable identifiers and re-check the sccs strings in the release you use. Same superfamily means SCOP judges a probable common evolutionary origin from structure and shared features: a common Rossmann-like βαβ nucleotide-binding core and a conserved dinucleotide-binding mode. That is a deeper and weaker relationship than same family. SCOPe families group clearer relationships, such as sequence-detectable homology or close functional and structural similarity. The separate families therefore signal clear divergence in sequence, function and often substrate and cofactor chemistry. A biologist should not read the shared superfamily as shared function, shared cofactor specificity or a shared catalytic mechanism. The ADH-like domain is the NAD(P)-binding half of zinc-dependent alcohol dehydrogenases and related medium-chain dehydrogenases/reductases, an oxidoreductase catalytic role. The CoA-binding domain is found in succinyl-CoA synthetase-type proteins and related proteins. Its Rossmann-like fold is used for CoA or nucleotide binding, not as a classic NAD(P) redox domain. The potassium channel NAD-binding domain, an RCK-type regulatory domain such as the Rck domain of Kch, is a ligand-sensing regulatory module of an ion channel. It is not an oxidoreductase catalytic domain. So the same fold can give redox catalysis, CoA-related enzymology, or ligand-gated regulation. Practical limits: do not transfer EC numbers, substrate, cofactor preference, catalytic residues or active-site annotation across these families on SCOPe placement alone. Do not use a member of one family as a modelling template for another's function or ligand-binding details. Backbone-level modelling of the core may be reasonable, but loops, the domain's role in the whole protein, oligomerisation and ligand-binding residues will differ. Superfamily membership alone is not evidence of orthology, and fold-level c.2 similarity would be weaker still. Check family-specific evidence before drawing conclusions: sequence alignment and conserved motifs (for example the Gly-rich dinucleotide-binding loop and acidic residue binding the ribose), HMM or profile hits, structure comparison, domain architecture, ligand-bound structures, and functional assays or literature. Also check whether the SCOPe domain is a single domain of a multidomain protein (ADH has a separate catalytic domain; the channel domain sits in a larger channel complex), since the function belongs to the whole protein context. When choosing representatives, pick one per family and not one per superfamily, since the families differ in function.
